abstract: Proteins operating beyond the plasma membrane are central to how plants build and remodel their cell walls, acquire and redistribute nutrients, coordinate developmental processes, and communicate between cells and tissues. Moreover, the reach of this extracellular proteome extends beyond the plant itself, with root and seed exudates shaping the rhizosphere and spermosphere by providing molecular signals and resources that influence microbial communities even before pathogens or symbionts establish direct contact with the plant surface. The extracellular space is therefore a dynamic biological interface connecting processes within the plant to interactions with the soil, microbiome, and broader environment. Despite this central role, the plant extracellular proteome remains fragmented across experimental approaches. Here, we review current techniques for the collection and purification of major plant extracellular fractions and use a uniform prediction pipeline to assess representative publicly available datasets. This analysis reveals consistent fraction-specific patterns in predicted secretion-class composition, with putative unconventional-secretion candidates exceeding canonical candidates in most fractions. We then present a decision tree linking biological questions to appropriate collection and fractionation strategies, together with complementary experimental criteria for assessing extracellular origin that extend beyond sequence-based prediction. Together, these resources provide a framework for interpreting existing extracellular proteomic datasets and for designing future studies that account for the biological distinctness of individual extracellular fractions. They are intended both as an entry point to plant extracellular proteomics and as a reference framework for improving the biological interpretation and comparability of studies across this diverse extracellular landscape.
